opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's helpful to look at how memory works in humans. We have something like working memory, which is roughly what the context window is doing in these models: it's quite short-term, it's whatever you're holding in your head right now. Then we have the cortex, which learns slowly over long periods, and that's somewhat analogous to the weights of the network being trained on huge amounts of data. But in between, there's this other system, the hippocampus, which is very good at rapidly picking up specific experiences, sometimes from a single exposure, and then over time that gets consolidated into the more general knowledge in the cortex.

Current models don't really have that middle piece. They've got the context window and they've got the trained weights, but there isn't a good mechanism for learning something specific quickly and then retaining it and integrating it over time. That's why you see these systems struggle with things like learning a new skill from just a few examples, or remembering something you told them last week.

But I don't see any fundamental reason why that can't be built. It's an architectural and algorithmic question, and people are already working on it in various ways: retrieval-based approaches, longer contexts, different kinds of memory modules, continual learning methods. None of them is fully satisfying yet, but these feel like normal research problems rather than some deep conceptual barrier. We know it's possible, because the brain does it, and we have a reasonable idea of the shape of the solution. So I'd expect this to be addressed, and when it is, I think it will make these systems a lot more capable, particularly at learning on the fly the way people do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts short-term context-window memory and slowly learned network weights with a missing mechanism for rapidly learning and retaining specific experiences.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible memory approaches and the brain analogy, but does not credit scalable model building with some understanding for opening new paths to address shortcomings.

r003.rationale: It expects the episodic-memory gap to be addressed through research, but does not claim that most language-model shortcomings can probably be adequately solved.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's worth being clear about what the gap actually is. Current models are very good at the kind of learning that happens slowly, over enormous amounts of data, where you compress the statistics of the world into the weights. That's a bit like our cortex gradually learning the structure of language or vision over years. What they don't have is the fast, one-shot thing that the hippocampus does, where something happens to you once, and you can recall it tomorrow, and it influences how you behave. The context window is a kind of crude substitute for that, but it's not really the same thing. It's a buffer, not a memory.

The reason I'm fairly optimistic is that this doesn't look like a fundamental barrier to me. It looks like an engineering and architecture problem, and we've already got a lot of the pieces. We know how to build retrieval systems. We know how to have a model write things down and read them back. We know from neuroscience that the brain solves this with a complementary learning system, a fast store and a slow store that consolidate over time, and that's a pretty good blueprint. Nobody has yet put it all together in a way that's clean and scales, but I don't see any argument that it can't be done. It's not like we're waiting on some new scientific principle.

I'd also say the history here is instructive. Ten years ago people said these systems couldn't do multi-step reasoning, couldn't handle long contexts, couldn't use tools. Each of those turned out to be a matter of working on it, rather than a wall. Episodic memory is on my list of things you'd need for something I'd be willing to call general intelligence, and it's one of the ones I'd expect to fall relatively soon, precisely because the shape of the solution is already visible. The harder questions are around what you store, how you decide what's important, and how you integrate it back into the slow weights without wrecking them. Those are real research problems, but they're the kind you make progress on by trying things, and a lot of people are now trying things.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts slow learning encoded in model weights with one-shot episodic learning, and describes the context window as a crude substitute for that fast memory.

r002.rationale: It mentions retrieval systems and architecture as pieces of a solution, but does not credit scalable model building with some understanding as opening new paths to address language-model shortcomings.

r003.rationale: It expresses optimism about episodic memory and cites several past capabilities that improved, but does not say that most existing language-model shortcomings can probably be solved through further research.

astra-6.text:
I don’t see a fundamental reason why we couldn’t solve it. With a human, you can have a conversation, go away, and come back a week later, and you remember something about that conversation. With a language model, unless you put the conversation back into its context, it’s essentially gone. That’s a significant limitation, but it seems like a limitation of how we’ve built these systems rather than some fundamental property of neural networks.

You can already imagine the ingredients: a system that stores experiences, retrieves the relevant ones, and uses them when deciding what to do. The difficult part is making that work well. What should it remember? What should it forget? When should it retrieve something, and how should that memory affect its answer? Simply attaching a database doesn’t solve all of those problems.

But those are concrete research questions. We don’t need to discover an entirely new principle of intelligence to start making progress on them. So I’m optimistic, although that’s different from saying we have the complete solution today.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts remembering within the context with a conversation being gone later, but it does not identify slower learning through base-model training.

r002.rationale: It describes memory mechanisms as possible research directions, but does not credit scalable model-building with understanding as opening new paths to address language-model shortcomings.

r003.rationale: It is optimistic about addressing episodic memory, but does not say that most existing language-model shortcomings can probably be adequately solved through further research.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t see a fundamental reason why we couldn’t solve it. These systems can already take information in context and use it quite effectively. What they’re missing is a way to retain the right information over time, retrieve it when it becomes relevant, and integrate it into what they’re doing.

You could imagine simply recording everything, but then you have the problem of deciding what to bring back into context. What matters? What’s related to the situation you’re in now? And when do you need the details of an experience versus some general lesson from it? Those are substantial research problems, but they seem like problems we can make progress on.

So I wouldn’t claim that you just bolt on a database and you’re done. But I also wouldn’t take the absence of episodic memory in today’s models as evidence that it’s somehow beyond this approach.

r001.rationale: It contrasts using information in context with retaining and retrieving it over time, but does not identify the gap as one between immediate context-window learning and slower base-model training.

r002.rationale: It does not credit scalable model building or explain how it opened new paths to address language-model shortcomings.

r003.rationale: It says research may solve the episodic-memory problem, but does not extend that view to most existing language-model shortcomings.
